policies.summary: Missouri has no siting statute specific to wind or solar. By the statute's text, any electrical corporation (any person owning or operating an electric plant to sell power to others, other than municipal utilities and rural cooperatives) needs Public Service Commission approval before building an electric plant, except an energy generation unit of 1 MW or less, and cities and counties also regulate land use through their general zoning powers.

restrictions.description: Commissioners cited possible effects on water, power, noise, drainage, and public health from large new solar, wind, battery-storage, and data-center developments outside city limits, describing the pause as 'due diligence'; no specific project was pending at the time of adoption. Active as of 2026-09-23; set to expire 2027-09-08 absent a single permitted extension of up to six additional months. Residents and at least one local business owner (who called the measure 'backdoor zoning') have publicly questioned whether the county had legal authority to adopt it without voter-approved planning and zoning; commissioners have declined to comment publicly and the county's own attorney has not returned press inquiries. Legal basis: Cedar County ordinance imposing a 12-month moratorium, adopted by commissioners 2026-09-08, citing (among other authority) RSMo §49.650 and county public-health authority; legal commentators note §49.650 by its terms applies to first-, second-, and fourth-class noncharter counties while Cedar County is third class, raising an open legal question about the ordinance's validity.

Pause on accepting, processing, or issuing permits, licenses, and applications for new data centers and battery energy storage systems while the city develops zoning and regulatory standards. Active as of 2026-09-23 (the 180-day moratorium is set to run through 2027-01-02 absent extension). Permanent data-center/BESS zoning rules remain in process: the City Council discussed proposed new standards but pushed its final vote back at least a month after confusion among residents and councilmembers, with City Manager Troy Anderson confirming the moratorium itself is unaffected by that separate vote; Mayor Kevin King said he would look into organizing a public hearing before the council revisits the permanent rules in October 2026. Similar temporary pauses remain in effect in unincorporated Jackson County and neighboring Leavenworth County, Kansas. Legal basis: Resolution No. 7238 (City Council agenda item 26-741), 'A resolution declaring a 180-day moratorium on the processing of applications related to and issuance of city permits or licenses related to the installation or use of data processing and hosting facilities located in the City of Independence, Missouri, for projects or applications not already submitted to, authorized, or approved by the City,' sponsored by Councilmember Stewart and passed 7-0 on 2026-07-06. A companion Resolution No. 7239 (agenda item 26-742) imposed a parallel 180-day moratorium on battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities, also passed 7-0 the same night.

Rapid emergence of data center and battery energy storage system applications; perceived gaps in the Jackson County Unified Development Code; infrastructure, environmental, public safety, and public notice concerns. Adopted by the County Legislature (8 in favor, 1 excused) on 2026-06-22 as a 180-day moratorium on data-center and BESS land-use applications, for the purpose of developing long-term policy, County Code provisions, and enhanced public-notice requirements. Whether the measure was signed by County Executive Phil LeVota, became law without signature, or was vetoed was not independently confirmed in this pass; no veto was reported in any subsequent coverage found. Legal basis: Ordinance 6074, introduced 2026-04-06 by Legislator Sean E. Smith (120-day version); a competing 365-day version (Ordinance 6087, sponsored by Legislative Chair Manny Abarca) was also considered in committee as of 2026-06-01. The full County Legislature passed a 180-day moratorium on data-center and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) land-use applications by an 8-1 vote (one member excused) on 2026-06-22. Per KCTV5, the ordinance then went to County Executive Phil LeVota, who had 10 days to sign or veto; no veto was reported in subsequent coverage found in this pass, but the Executive's signature was not independently confirmed, and the exact ordinance/file number of the version that received final passage (whether an amended Ordinance 6074 or a substitute) was not confirmed from a primary Legistar record, which returned an access error to automated fetch.

Stone County Planning Commission cited 'considerable interest and concern on the part of residents' about possible development of solar, wind, battery-storage, and data-center projects in unincorporated Stone County, and sought time to consider amendments to the county Zoning Regulations. Active as of 2026-09-23; set to expire 2027-06-04 absent extension or earlier replacement by amended zoning regulations. Legal basis: Stone County Order and Ordinance enacting a temporary 12-month moratorium, adopted by the County Commission 2026-06-04 pursuant to a Stone County Planning Commission resolution adopted 2026-06-02, under RSMo §§64.800-64.905 (county planning/zoning) and §§64.860 and 64.875.

County study of legal authority and potential impacts of data centers, solar, wind, and battery energy storage system facilities in unincorporated Webster County. Active per primary county order. Legal basis: Order 2026-03.
